title: a library that tells one story
hookLine: not one book but a shelf of them, read as one story from a garden to a city
tomorrow: you've said it a thousand times
last: COMMUNION · TRINITY · BORN AGAIN · BAPTISM · TESTIMONY · HOLY SPIRIT

cards: It's in a hotel drawer, on a phone app, in a grandmother's lap with the pages gone soft. It's easy to picture one thick book.

Open the table of contents, though, and it's a whole shelf: poems, letters, laws, family stories, songs of complaint, four lives of Jesus. Written over many centuries, by many hands. And Christians read it as one story.

teach.b: The word Bible comes from the Greek ta biblia: the books. Plural. A library.
If you've ever started on page one and gotten lost somewhere in the laws, that's why: nobody reads a library front to back, and a lot of people start with one of the Gospels instead.
Protestant Bibles have sixty-six books, Catholic Bibles seventy-three, Orthodox Bibles a few more. There are two big parts. The Old Testament is the Jewish scriptures, the ones Jesus himself read.
The New Testament was written by his first followers.
Testament means covenant: a binding promise. Here's a surprise. The chapter and verse numbers aren't original.
Chapters came in the 1200s, and the New Testament's verse numbers in the 1500s, so for most of Christian history nobody could look up day three's verse as John 3:16.

Then the shape. Many Christians tell it in a few big moves: a world made good, a family chosen, slaves set free, kings and prophets, exile and return, then Jesus, and his followers sent out. And the bookends.
Near the very start there's a garden with a tree of life. On the last page, the tree of life is back, growing beside a river in a city made new. The story ends where it began.

how: Christians read the Bible aloud in church services, often from both Testaments, and many read it at home through a daily plan or an app; churches differ on which books belong in the Old Testament (66 books in Protestant Bibles, 73 in Catholic, more in Orthodox).

games.q: near the start of the Bible there's a garden with a tree of life. where does that tree show up again?
o: on the last page, beside a river in a city made new.
games.why: the story ends where it began, made new: the tree of life is back on the Bible's last page.

games.q: put the big moves of the story in order.

practice: Three breaths with the bell. On the first, think of where your own story started. On the second, think of a chapter that was hard.
On the third, picture one thing you hope gets made new. Three breaths, one story.
